concepts.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
concepts.definition: Planets obey three empirical rules: each moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; the line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times; and the square of the orbital period grows with the cube of the semi-major axis across all planets of the Sun.
concepts.key_idea: Equal areas in equal times is the fingerprint of a central force -- and the period law fixed the inverse-square form of gravity.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph107.txt lines 40-140 (section 7.2 Kepler's laws, ellipse with sun at focus, area law, period squared versus semi-major axis cubed)
question_patterns: state Kepler's three laws of planetary motion

solution_steps.explain: Every planet travels an ellipse with the Sun at one focus -- circles are just special ellipses.
The Sun-planet line sweeps equal areas in equal intervals, so the planet speeds up near the Sun and slows far away.
Across the planets, the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, a relation Newton later derived from his law of gravitation.

concepts.title: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
concepts.definition: Every pair of masses attracts along the line joining them with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. The fixed proportionality constant is the universal gravitational constant G, the same for any two bodies anywhere in the universe.
concepts.key_idea: One formula, one constant, everything from falling apples to orbiting moons -- attraction scales with masses and dies with distance squared.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph107.txt lines 141-260 (sections 7.3 universal law of gravitation, 7.4 gravitational constant G, inverse square rule, vector form)

solution_steps.explain: The inverse square rule needs the distance squared in the denominator.
Multiply G by both masses and divide by the squared separation.

concepts.title: Acceleration Due to Gravity and Its Variation
concepts.definition: Gravity's pull at a planet's surface sets g = G M over R squared. Moving up reduces g by the factor (1 + h/R) squared, while descending into mines reduces it in proportion to depth because only the mass below you still attracts. Thus g weakens both on mountains and underground, though differently.
concepts.key_idea: g shrinks with altitude through the inverse square and with depth through the shrinking enclosed mass -- height costs faster.

concepts.title: Escape Speed from a Planet
concepts.definition: To break free of a planet's gravity starting from its surface, a body needs a launch speed that makes its kinetic energy just pay off the gravitational debt: v equals the square root of twice G M over R, which also reads as the square root of twice g R. For earth this is about 11.2 km per second, independent of the projectile's mass.
concepts.key_idea: Escape speed equals the speed gained by falling from infinity -- about 11.2 km/s from earth, mass never enters.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph107.txt lines 381-460 (section 7.8 escape speed, energy argument, escape speed from the earth 11.2 km/s)

solution_steps.explain: The energy balance squares the escape speed to twice g R.
The root is the escape speed.

concepts.title: Earth Satellites: Orbital Speed, Period and Weightlessness
concepts.definition: A satellite in circular orbit rides gravity as its centripetal force, giving orbital speed as the square root of G M over orbit radius and a period that grows with orbit size. An astronaut falls with the spacecraft at the same rate, so no contact force presses on her -- the sensation of weightlessness.
concepts.key_idea: Orbiting is perpetual free fall -- gravity bends the path into a circle while the satellite feels no floor.
concepts.textbook_ref: keph107.txt lines 461-580 (sections 7.9 earth satellites, orbital velocity and period, 7.10 energy of an orbiting satellite, weightlessness)

solution_steps.action: divide GM by the orbit radius
solution_steps.explain: The ratio G M over orbit radius equals the square of the orbital speed.
The root is the orbital speed.
